newsitem.title: USA: Dismal pricing outlook seen for US paper companies.
newsitem.headline: Dismal pricing outlook seen for US paper companies.

text.p: Weak paper and pulp prices could pull down U.S. paper companies' earnings in the first quarter, just as they depressed recently-announced fourth-quarter results, analysts said on Monday.
"We're looking at a very weak first quarter," Mark Wilde, an analyst at Bankers Trust, said.
Most paper companies have reported sharply lower fourth quarter earnings -- as expected -- compared to strong fourth quarter 1995 results, blaming lower pulp and paper prices.
Analysts said soft prices stemmed from plant overcapacity, higher mill inventories, lower demand, a stronger dollar and higher energy costs, which compressed margins.

"Paper and forest product earnings have been declining steadily through 1996 and there was no interruption in the fourth quarter," Cornelius Sewell, an analyst at Argus Research, said. "Business is lousy."
Nor do they see much improvement before the spring.
"It is going to be a slow, uneven and, for some grades, painful recovery," an analyst said.

Paper prices going into 1997 were below the fourth-quarter average, analysts said, pointing to recent declines in the price of containerboard, newsprint, coated paper and uncoated freesheet. The pricing environment would not improve until at least the second quarter, they said.
"The fourth quarter 1996 and the first quarter 1997 should be the earnings trough, as demand improves and inventories get worked off," Mark Diverio, an analyst at UBS Securities, said.
Bellwether International Paper Co reported a loss of $0.02 per share in its fourth quarter compared to a profit of $1.01 per share in the year-earlier quarter.
Champion International earned $0.11 per share in the fourth quarter compared with $2.26 per share in the same year-earlier quarter.
Georgia-Pacific Corp reported fourth-quarter earnings of $0.02 per share versus $2.17 per share in the fourth quarter 1995.

The company said its results were hurt by a "collapse" in prices for most markets. Its pulp and paper business reported 1996 operating profits of $390 million, compared with profits of $1.6 billion in 1995.
Boise Cascade Corp Chairman George Harad said the company's results for the 1996 fourth quarter and full year reflected unfavorable paper market conditions.
Harad said for early 1997, paper prices remained depressed.

BT Securities' Wilde said: "On the paperboard side -- the biggest market there is containerboard -- those prices are slipping again... And on the paper side, we are going to have a quarter-to-quarter decline for the first quarter in the price of newsprint, coated paper and white office paper, or uncoated free sheet."
Wilde also said the pulp market could also suffer a bit because inventories had gone up again. But he recommended buying some paper stocks ahead of a pricing recovery.

"Supply is still exceeding demand, although demand is not too bad," said Smith Barney analyst George Adler. "We either need to move volume up or companies need to take more downtime." He forecast 1997 earnings for the paper companies would be higher than 1996 results.
"But we need better prices to get there," he said.
Other paper companies due to report earnings this week included Union Camp Corp, Stone Container Corp, Temple-Inland Inc, Louisiana-Pacific Corp and Weyerhaeuser Co.
